blocks.title: Separate available parallel work from hardware capacity
paragraphs: Parallel execution needs independent work and hardware able to carry it out. A processor count is not itself a speedup: some work may be serial, some may contend for resources, and coordination can add cost.
Classify the work first. Instruction-level overlap uses independent operations; data parallelism applies similar operations to different data; task parallelism runs different tasks.

blocks.title: Compare execution models with the workload in view
paragraphs: A superscalar implementation can issue multiple eligible instructions; multicore systems provide multiple processing cores; GPU-style execution emphasizes substantial data-parallel work. These descriptions do not establish that a workload can use the available parallelism.

Compare dependencies, data movement, branching and synchronization. A wide parallel machine can be poorly utilized by a small serial task. Explain what work can run concurrently rather than ranking labels as inherently faster.

blocks.title: Derive speedup from normalized time
paragraphs: Let s be the serial fraction of the original one-processor execution time and p the processor count. With ideal scaling of the remaining fraction and no overhead, relative time is s+(1−s)/p. Speedup is its reciprocal.
Keep the baseline fixed: s is a fraction of original execution time, not a fraction of processors. If overhead or contention is included, add its stated time rather than assuming ideal scaling.

blocks.title: A serial quarter limits three processors
paragraphs: For s=1/4 and p=3, relative time is 1/4+(3/4)/3 = 1/2. Speedup is 2. With unlimited processors the parallel part tends toward zero but the serial quarter remains, so the upper bound is 4.

For the same ideal model, observed speedup S=2 at p=3 implies s=(1/S−1/p)/(1−1/p) = (1/2−1/3)/(2/3) = 1/4. The inference is conditional on the model; measured overhead can invalidate that interpretation.

blocks.title: Check the boundary cases
paragraphs: With one processor, speedup is 1. With all work serial, extra processors do not help. With zero serial fraction and no overhead, ideal speedup equals processor count; there is no finite serial-fraction ceiling.
Real speedup may be lower because data movement, synchronization, imbalance or resource contention adds time. Amdahl’s simple calculation is a stated model, not a forecast of a particular device.

blocks.title: Explain the execution model and then calculate
paragraphs: Identify the form of parallelism and whether the workload exposes it. Normalize the baseline time, divide only the parallel fraction and retain the serial fraction.
Use the Amdahl workspace to explore boundaries and Practice to check a fixed calculation plus an unscored architecture comparison.

cards.prompt: How do data and task parallelism differ?
cards.answer: Data parallelism applies similar operations across different data; task parallelism executes different tasks. Both still need safe independence and sufficient resources.

cards.prompt: Why does more parallel hardware not guarantee useful speedup?
cards.answer: Dependencies, workload size, data movement, imbalance and coordination can limit utilization. Hardware capacity and exploitable parallel work are separate.

cards.prompt: Which part of execution time is divided by p in the ideal Amdahl model?
cards.answer: Only the original parallel fraction: relative time=s+(1−s)/p. Speedup is 1 divided by that time.

cards.prompt: What is Amdahl’s limit when the serial fraction s is positive?
cards.answer: As processor count grows, speedup approaches 1/s. For s=0 the ideal model has no finite serial ceiling.

guided.title: Match hardware to work
guided.prompt: Compare a dependency-heavy sequential task with many independent applications of one operation to data. Explain what each can exploit without predicting device speed.
rubric: Identify limited instruction/task independence in the sequential case.
Identify data parallelism in the repeated independent operation.
Discuss data movement and coordination before making a performance claim; multiple reasoned comparisons can satisfy the task.
